missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain methods used to measure human reaction times and recall typical results
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson recalls typical results (0.2–0.9 s) but never describes a way to measure reaction time, such as the ruler-drop test or a computer test.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret and evaluate measurements from simple methods to measure the different reaction times of students
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson contains no reaction-time measurements to interpret or evaluate. It also does not discuss repeat readings, averages or reliability.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: evaluate the effect of various factors on thinking distance based on given data.
missing_spec_content.why: The factors are listed qualitatively. The student is never given data, for example reaction times with and without a distraction, to evaluate.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (Physics only) Students will be required to interpret graphs relating speed to stopping distance for a range of vehicles.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson has a table for cars only. There are no graphs and no other vehicle types (for example lorries or bicycles).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (Physics only) Students should be able to estimate how the distance for a vehicle to make an emergency stop varies over a range of speeds typical for that vehicle.
missing_spec_content.why: The table gives standard car values. The student is not shown how to estimate stopping distances, and other vehicles are not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson treats braking force as constant and varies the distance. It never states the spec's point that a higher speed needs a larger braking force to stop in the same distance.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.
missing_spec_content.why: Overheating is covered, but loss of control (for example skidding) as a danger of large decelerations is never mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) estimate the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles in typical situations on a public road.
missing_spec_content.why: F = ma is stated, but there is no estimate of a typical braking force from a typical car mass and deceleration (or from speed and stopping distance).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.
missing_spec_content.why: The main lesson text never states that the work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy. This only appears in a tutor_note. The keyTerms definition of friction refers only to tyre and road.

above_gcse.text: The UK legal minimum tyre tread depth is 1.6 mm.
above_gcse.why: This is a legal fact, not specification content.

above_gcse.text: severe tiredness can cause microsleep at the wheel
above_gcse.why: Microsleep is not in the specification. The spec only says tiredness affects reaction time.

above_gcse.text: Braking distance = KE ÷ braking force. This gives the quadratic relationship.
above_gcse.why: The spec only requires that a greater speed gives a greater stopping distance for a given braking force. The quantitative v² derivation goes beyond these sections. It is not wrong.

wrong_terms.text: The kinetic energy of the car is transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes through friction.
wrong_terms.spec_term: work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases

wrong_terms.text: The force between tyre and road surface that allows braking
wrong_terms.spec_term: friction force between the brakes and the wheel
